content: Infants demonstrate a remarkable ability to make strong ontological inferences about the nature of the world and the types of entities it contains. Developmental psychology has extensively studied the stages at which these metaphysical understandings are acquired. Infants infer that the world is composed of rigid objects that maintain continuity in both space and time. They perceive any surface that is cohesive, bounded, and moves as a single unit to be a distinct object. When they observe one solid object seemingly passing through another, they exhibit surprise, indicating an expectation of physical consistency. By the time they are less than a year old, infants can differentiate between causal and non-causal events, even when these events share similar spatial and temporal characteristics. They also distinguish between objects that require external forces to move (inanimate objects) and those capable of self-generated motion (animate objects). Infants assume that the self-propelled movement of animate objects is driven by invisible internal states, such as goals and intentions. These internal states, while not directly observable, are inferred by the infant based on the behavior of the object. When an adult points to a novel object and utters a word-like sound, toddlers tend to assume that the sound refers to the entire object rather than one of its individual parts. However, some of these cognitive inferences may not develop in infants with autism, suggesting differences in the acquisition of metaphysical understanding. In newborns, sensory data are processed but do not yet carry meaning, and they lack the ability to differentiate between themselves and the external world. Psychologists widely agree that self-awareness does not emerge until mid-childhood and is present in only a limited number of animal species. A common test for self-awareness involves placing a mark, such as a dot, on the subject's body and observing their reaction when they see themselves in a mirror. If the subject investigates the mark, it suggests an awareness of their own existence. In contrast, many species interpret the reflection as another animal rather than themselves. Object permanence, the understanding that objects continue to exist even when they are not visible, is a critical milestone in an infant's cognitive development. Experiments to assess object permanence often involve hiding a toy behind a barrier and then revealing it repeatedly, as in the game of peekaboo. During the early sensorimotor stages, infants are unable to grasp the concept of object permanence. Jean Piaget's experiments with infants led him to conclude that this awareness typically develops around eight to nine months of age. Before this stage, infants do not cry when their mothers leave because they lack the understanding that their mothers continue to exist when out of sight, a phenomenon often summarized as out of sight, out of mind. A lack of object permanence can result in A-not-B errors, where children search for an object in a location where it was previously found, even when they have seen it moved to a new location. Additionally, recent psychological studies suggest that the perception of three-dimensionality is not innate but must be learned during infancy through unconscious inference, a process that underlies the development of depth perception.
